---
title: "Explore AR, ARX, and recurrent models"
toc: false
page-layout: full
---

The [Silverbox benchmark](https://www.nonlinearbenchmark.org/benchmarks/silverbox)
is a measured electronic system designed to behave like a Duffing oscillator:
a system with dynamics and a nonlinear restoring effect. It has one applied
input, `V1`, and one measured response, `V2`. For a mechanical analogy, think
of `V1` as a force-like excitation and `V2` as a displacement-like response.

Because `V1` is deliberately applied to the physical system, its relation to
`V2` is causal rather than a generic feature--target association:

```{=html}
<div class="silverbox-system-map silverbox-system-map-intro" aria-label="Causal relationship from applied input V1 to measured response V2">
  <div class="silverbox-system-map-item silverbox-system-map-input">
    <span>Applied causal input</span>
    <strong><code>V1</code> = <em>u</em><sub>t</sub></strong>
  </div>
  <span class="silverbox-system-map-arrow" aria-hidden="true"><span>drives</span><b>→</b></span>
  <div class="silverbox-system-map-item silverbox-system-map-core">
    <span>Silverbox</span>
    <strong>nonlinear dynamics</strong>
  </div>
  <span class="silverbox-system-map-arrow" aria-hidden="true"><span>produces</span><b>→</b></span>
  <div class="silverbox-system-map-item silverbox-system-map-output">
    <span>Measured response</span>
    <strong><code>V2</code> = <em>y</em><sub>t</sub></strong>
  </div>
</div>
```

Our task is to predict the next response from information available at that
time. The models below make different assumptions about how the recent input
and response determine that prediction.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{AR:}\qquad
\widehat{y}_t
&= \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j y_{t-j}, \\
\text{ARX:}\qquad
\widehat{y}_t
&= \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j y_{t-j}
   + \sum_{j=0}^{p}\gamma_j u_{t-j}, \\
\text{Response-only RNN:}\qquad
h_t
&= \tanh\!\left(W_h h_{t-1} + W_y y_{t-1} + b_h\right),
\qquad \widehat{y}_t = W_o h_t + b_o, \\
\text{Input-aware RNN:}\qquad
h_t
&= \tanh\!\left(W_h h_{t-1} + W_y y_{t-1} + W_u u_t + b_h\right),
\qquad \widehat{y}_t = W_o h_t + b_o.
\end{aligned}
$$

All four models are fitted on the first 25,000 training samples, then begin the
held-out forecast with the last 20 responses of the complete training record.
The intervening training samples are not used for fitting or warmup.
AR and ARX retain those values explicitly as lag history. The two RNNs read
them in time order to prime learned hidden states, then carry those states
forward. Only the input-aware RNN receives the current known input alongside
its previous response forecast.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to watch

AR and the response-only RNN cannot react directly to a changing excitation
because neither sees `V1`; moving from AR to a response-only RNN changes the
representation of history, not the measured information. ARX and the
input-aware RNN can use the applied input. ARX uses a fixed list of lags in a
linear rule, whereas the input-aware RNN compresses earlier information into a
nonlinear state and carries that state from one forecast step to the next.
During training, backpropagation is truncated to manageable chunks, so this
does not mean that its gradients extend indefinitely into the past.
:::

```{=html}

      </div>
      <div>

      <div>

  </section>
</div>
```

This comparison separates two ideas: a nonlinear recurrent representation and
access to the known causal input. It does **not** establish that recurrence is
the only helpful idea: a nonlinear fixed-window model or a different recurrent
architecture would be useful additional comparisons.
